name: Rosa Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I'm not really a tech person so I don't know how much help I'll be, but I'll answer honestly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Gerry Doyle, who runs a small building firm doing repairs on old houses. Most days I'm fixing rotten sash windows, replacing floorboards or doing roof timbers, with Gerry and one other guy, Sam. I like the old houses, you open a wall and find newspaper from the 1950s. What wears me out is the dust and the lifting, and Gerry's van has no heating.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How steady does the work feel right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Steady-ish, as long as Gerry keeps going. He's 64 and he talks about retiring every winter. I've got less than a month's money saved and my partner Dev works in a parcel warehouse on the edge of town. There's only one other small builder round here, and they've got their own family working for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So no big change from AI. That's good, I suppose, nothing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, to be honest. People were making a fuss about nothing. I don't use any of it and I don't need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI isn't my worry anyway. My boss Gerry is 64 and keeps saying this is his last winter. When Gerry retires, I don't know who in this town would take me on. That's the thing that keeps me up, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Gerry as long as he goes. I'd try to put a bit aside each week, maybe thirty, and stop buying lunch from the bakery. I'd probably ask Gerry if he's thought about selling the firm to someone who'd keep us on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried, the same worry I've had for a year. AI being hype doesn't change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Gerry retired next spring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring round the bigger firms in the city, but that's an hour each way and I don't drive. Maybe I'd ask Sam if he wanted to carry on with me, but neither of us has money for a van. Honestly, I'd probably end up doing odd jobs for neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you talked to Gerry about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I don't want to push him. He's been good to me, he took me on when I finished my apprenticeship and nobody else would.

say: She's **glad** AI turned out to be a fuss about nothing.
She doesn't use any AI tools at work and **doesn't need** to.
think: Her real worry is her boss **Gerry retiring**, not computers.
Few other **builders** in her town would be likely to take her on.
do: Keep working for **Gerry** as long as he carries on.
Save about **thirty a week** by skipping bakery lunches.
Ask Gerry about **selling the firm** to someone who keeps the crew.
feel: The **same worry** she's had for a year, unchanged by AI.
S0.quote: My boss Gerry is 64 and keeps saying this is his last winter. When Gerry retires, I don't know who in this town would take me on.
fieldNote: Already **anxious** without AI: boss near retirement, thin savings, one other small builder in town.
Doesn't drive, which **narrows her options** to local work.
Loyal to Gerry and **avoids** raising the hard question with him.

steps.text: Keep repairing windows and floors for Gerry's firm
Save thirty a week by skipping bakery lunches
Wait to hear if Gerry will sell the firm before job hunting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so office stuff first, booking and ordering. Gerry does all that on a clipboard anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't touch us much, we're too small. Nobody's sending a robot to fix a sash window in a terraced house. I'd say it's a big-company thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in a parcel warehouse are coming before robots on a roof, so my partner Dev's job worries me more than mine. Dev's bosses already talk about machines that sort parcels. If he loses hours, we can't cover the rent on my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. I'd tell Dev to look around now, maybe the hospital porter jobs, while there's still time. And we'd cut back, no takeaways, cancel the TV package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried for us as a household. I'm not panicking, but I'd be checking our bank app more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Gerry wanted to try an app to do his quotes, would you help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave it to Sam, he's better with phones. I'd carry on with my notebook. I know that's stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if Dev's hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, then the takeaways, then visiting my sister in the city, because the train is expensive. We'd keep the rent and the electric paid no matter what. I've never missed rent and I'm not starting.

say: The change won't touch **small firms** like Gerry's much.
Nobody's sending a robot to fix a **sash window** in a terraced house.
think: Robots in **parcel warehouses** come before robots on roofs.
If Dev loses hours, her pay alone can't cover the **rent**.
do: Keep working at Gerry's firm with her **head down**.
Tell Dev to apply for **hospital porter** jobs now.
feel: Worried for the **household**, checking the bank app more often.
S1.quote: Robots in a parcel warehouse are coming before robots on a roof, so my partner Dev's job worries me more than mine.
fieldNote: Her own job looks safe, but Dev's **warehouse job** makes the household **anxious**.
Leaves any new tech to **Sam**, true to her resistance.
Pride in **never missing rent** drives her spending choices.

steps.text: Keep working with Gerry and use her paper notebook
Help Dev apply for hospital porter jobs
Cancel the TV package, gym and takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people by 2031? That's not long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. People have been saying robots will build houses for years. I wouldn't want to scare anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if it's true, I'm finished in this job by about 2031. I keep all my measurements in a paper notebook. By 2031 a robot won't need a notebook, or me. And Dev would probably go before me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Gerry for as long as there's work and save everything I can. I'd move in with Dev's parents to save on rent if things got bad. I'd look at care work or hospital cleaning, something with people, but I'd probably wait too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd feel sick, like when you hear a bad noise from the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait too long. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I do. I don't like change, and I'd tell myself it might not happen. Then it would happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need to sit down with his mum and dad and be honest. They've got a spare room. I'd hate it, but it's better than being on the street.

say: She'd say she won't **believe it** until she sees it.
She wouldn't want to **scare** anyone at work.
think: She'd be **finished** in her carpentry job by about 2031.
Dev would probably lose his **warehouse job** even before she lost hers.
do: Keep working for Gerry and **save everything** possible.
Move in with **Dev's parents** if money runs out.
Look at **care or hospital cleaning** work, though likely too late.
feel: **Scared** and sick, like hearing a bad noise from the roof.
S2.quote: I keep all my measurements in a paper notebook. By 2031 a robot won't need a notebook, or me.
fieldNote: Public **disbelief** hides private certainty that both incomes go.
Admits she'd **wait too long**, which makes the outlook worse.
Falls back on **family**, Dev's parents' spare room, as the safety net.

steps.text: Save every spare pound while Gerry still has work
Move in with Dev's parents if the rent can't be paid
Hold off job hunting until robots actually reach old-house repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the same, but robots in 2034. Five years more or less of normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and the government should sort out some sensible help. I'd say it calmly, I don't like people shouting about it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years would just give me more time to pretend it isn't happening, and I know that about myself. I'd keep working and keep telling myself next year. The end is still the same, I'd be 35 with no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving, aiming for two months' rent. I'd maybe ask Gerry to put me on the quotes side, so I learn a bit of the business. And I'd vote for whoever has a practical plan for retraining, not the shouting ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried. It's a slow worry, but it's there every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Gerry said he was closing up, that would push me. Or if Dev got laid off. Without a push, I'd stay put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would quoting still matter by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, now you say it, since the computers would do quotes. I just thought it'd make me more useful to Gerry. I don't have a better idea.

say: There's **time**, and the government should offer some **sensible help**.
She'd say it calmly, without **shouting** about it either way.
think: Five years gives her more time to **pretend** it isn't happening.
The **end point** is the same: aged 35 with no other trade.
do: Ask Gerry to teach her the **quotes** side.
feel: A **slow worry** that's there every day.
S3.quote: Five years would just give me more time to pretend it isn't happening, and I know that about myself.
fieldNote: Extra time doesn't calm her because she **won't act** without a push.
Picks **quoting** as a skill, then sees AI would take that too.
Centre outlook shows in wanting **practical**, not loud, politics.

steps.text: Ask Gerry to teach her how he prices jobs
Vote for the party with a practical retraining plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for the robots. I'd be about 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off and lots can change. I'd tell people not to panic. I'd probably say the same thing I'd say about the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one I can live with. Old houses are crooked and every one is different. A robot would have to be very clever to fix a two-hundred-year-old window. I might get ten more years of the work I love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working with Gerry, or whoever takes his firm on. I'd save slowly and try to get a driving licence so I could work further away. And I'd think about care work in my thirties, when I'm worn out from lifting anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Still a bit uneasy, but it's far enough away to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a driving licence now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can only work where the bus goes, and that's the town. With a licence I could get to the city firms. I've put it off for years because lessons cost money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, tight. Gerry might go, Dev's warehouse might change. Ten years for robots doesn't fix that.

say: Ten years is a **long way off** and lots can change.
People shouldn't **panic** about it, any more than about the weather.
think: Old **crooked houses** may protect her work for ten more years.
This is the picture she **can live with**.
do: Keep working for Gerry or whoever **takes over** his firm.
Get a **driving licence** to reach city firms.
feel: **Better**, with room to breathe, though still a bit uneasy.
S4.quote: Old houses are crooked and every one is different. A robot would have to be very clever to fix a two-hundred-year-old window.
fieldNote: Finds hope in the odd shapes of **old houses**, which robots would struggle with.
Mood stays **anxious** because Gerry's retirement and Dev's job are unchanged.
A **driving licence** is her first concrete step to widen her options.

steps.text: Keep doing old-house repairs for Gerry or his successor
Get a driving licence to reach building firms in the city
Save a little each month for driving lessons

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come by 2031, and Dev and I would both be out with nothing saved. What would help is a sensible plan from the government, like free courses near home and help with rent while you switch. Something practical, not promises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask the quiet ones. Nobody ever asks the people in the middle, who just want a steady job and a fair rent and don't shout about politics.

headlineQuote: Nobody ever asks the people in the middle, who just want a steady job and a fair rent and don't shout about politics.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old carpenter** repairing old houses for a small local builder.
Her boss Gerry is 64 and talks of **retiring**, and only one other small builder works locally.
She has **under a month** saved, doesn't drive, and her partner Dev works in a **warehouse**.
She never uses **AI**, keeps a paper notebook, and admits she waits too long to change.
Already **anxious**, she becomes **alarmed** in the faster AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Dev would both be out of **work** with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Free local courses** and help with rent while switching jobs.
